subject: Food Science
title: Umami: The Fifth Taste
description: A quick win: understand Umami: The Fifth Taste.

hook.text: Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda tasted kombu seaweed broth in 1908 and knew it wasn't sweet, salty, sour, or bitter.

buildup.text: Ikeda isolated glutamate as the source, then created monosodium glutamate (MSG) to replicate it.

discovery.text: Umami signals protein presence—essential for survival. Breast milk is rich in glutamate, making it one of the first tastes babies.

twist.text: Parmesan cheese contains 1,200 mg of glutamate per 100g—more than MSG seasoning. The most 'umami' food isn't Asian; it's Italian.

climax.text: Umami enhances other flavors and increases salivation. It makes food taste 'complete' and satisfying.

punchline.text: A fifth taste, hiding in plain sight for centuries. Parmesan has more than MSG.
